newsitem.title: USA: Clinton warmly welcomes anti-tobacco ruling.
newsitem.headline: Clinton warmly welcomes anti-tobacco ruling.

text.p: President Clinton Friday warmly welcomed a federal judge's ruling that nicotine can be regulated as a drug but said his administration would appeal one aspect of the court decision.
"This is on balance a great victory for the fight we have been waging for our children's health," Clinton told a news conference with visiting Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

In a major blow to the tobacco industry, U.S. District Judge William Osteen in Greensboro, N.C., found that cigarettes could be regulated as drug delivery devices under federal law and that the Food and Drug Administration can regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes.

"Here at the White House we see this as a tremendous victory for the American people," Vice President Al Gore said in an interview with wire service reporters. "It will be remembered in history as a turning point in the battle to protect our children."
The judge also ruled that the FDA could not police advertising and promotion of cigarettes -- a part of the ruling that Clinton said would be appealed by government lawyers.

"With this ruling, we can regulate tobacco products and protect our children from a lifetime of addiction and the prospect of having their lives cut short by the diseases that come with this addiction," Clinton said.
He set the litigation in motion in 1995 when he authorized the FDA to regulate cigarettes in a bid to curb smoking by children.
The White House has also been carefully monitoring talks between state attorneys general and lawyers for the tobacco industry representatives and plaintiffs who have sued the industry.
The negotiators met at the White House Wednesday with White House deputy counsel Bruce Lindsey.
Published reports have said the industry might pay as much as $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers who fall sick with lung cancer and other diseases.
In return, the tobacco industry would get broad shelter from lawsuits and higher stock market valuations on their thriving tobacco and non-smoking businesses.
Clinton said his opinion about any proposed settlements, "should one ever be agreed to, would be determined solely on what I thought was good for kids and good for the public health."
